A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Reverse Flow Matching work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original learning curves on eight DeepMind Control Suite environments, evaluated over five seeds in Figure 1.

after.justification: v2 reports original continuous-control results, two-moon sampling results, runtime comparisons, sensitivity studies, and ablations in Sections 5 and Appendix G.

M1.justification: Section 4.4 changes the RL instantiation from direct action-space flow to an unconstrained latent flow mapped through tanh, incorporating the Jacobian into the target density and posterior score. Training interpolants now use policy-generated endpoints instead of replay-buffer actions. These alter the specified procedure, while the general RFM framework remains.

E1.justification: The same eight continuous-control environments are retained. v2 adds a synthetic two-moon density-sampling task in Section 5.1; the additional RL analyses use existing environments rather than expanding the control-task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds QVPO to the main eight-task comparison, SDAC and DIME on two retained environments in Appendix G.3, and iDEM in the new toy comparison. v1 cited some of these methods without evaluating them. QNE's presentation as MaxEntDP in the RL comparison is matched as the retained comparator, not counted as an addition.

E3.justification: The new toy protocol compares equal posterior sample counts with 20 RFM versus 100 diffusion inference steps and evaluates SWD, MMD2, and Sinkhorn distance. Appendix G adds controlled sweeps of Monte Carlo samples, action candidates, and flow steps, plus alternate-proposal and soft-Q configurations. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v1 has no reported ablation or sensitivity experiments. v2 Appendix G tests estimated control-variate coefficients against fixed noise/gradient variants, compares proposal distributions and standard versus soft Q-functions, and studies sensitivity to sampling budgets and flow steps. The control-variate and proposal questions are examined in both RL and the toy task.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 1 reports means with 95% confidence intervals over five seeds; the corresponding v2 Figure 2 reports means with minimum-to-maximum ranges over five seeds. The uncertainty summary changes, with no reported increase in the seed count.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results absent from v1: toy discrepancies, ablation and sensitivity findings, additional baseline curves, and runtime measurements. Figure 1 reports RFM SWD of 0.113 versus 0.1311 for iDEM and 0.1768 for QNE, using 20 versus 100 inference steps. Table 2 reports training times of 15 minutes for RFM, 33 for DQS, and 30 for MaxEntDP. These are new evaluations, not matched-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: The main equivalence theorems, Stein identities, asymptotic variance minimization results, and reverse-score-matching proofs are retained, largely relocated to Appendices C–D. v2 adds the tanh-transformed target density and corresponding posterior-score derivation. It removes v1 Remark 2's simplified optimal coefficients for proposals equal to the posterior.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace v1's unqualified 'optimal, minimum-variance estimator' claim with an effective variance-reduced estimator, narrowing the headline optimality claim. The central contributions—posterior inference, unifying noise and gradient estimators, extending to flow policies, and strong continuous-control performance—remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds targeted interpretations: latent-space support satisfies the equivalence theorem's condition, proposal experiments suggest robustness, and soft-Q degradation may reflect numerical difficulty. It also qualifies toy superiority as a limited-computation finding because all variants can succeed with sufficient training. These refine the retained account of variance reduction and training stability.

D1.justification: Appendices E–F add an explicit sample-based coefficient estimator with ridge regularization, toy energy and proposal construction, metric settings, and detailed RL hyperparameters. Table 1 specifies architectures, learning rates, budgets, and candidate counts; v2 also identifies JAX, baseline implementation sources, hardware, and training times. These substantially improve documentation beyond v1's generic implementation statements.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for DIME, GenPO, GoRL, and entropy-regularized flow matching, and explicitly identifies the review's off-policy focus. The four-category organization and positioning around unifying noise-expectation and gradient-expectation methods remain. Publication metadata updates are not counted as new works.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the introduction into explicit contributions, compresses main-text related work while moving its detailed discussion to Appendix A, and relocates proofs to Appendix C. Reverse score matching moves from Appendix A to D, algorithm material moves to Appendix E, and experiments acquire separate toy/RL sections and detailed appendices. This substantially changes the reading structure.

P2.justification: v2 switches the main text to a two-column conference layout, redraws the main RL figure with revised legends and an added comparator, and relocates the algorithm display to the appendix. It adds six figures covering toy samples and supplementary experiments, plus hyperparameter and runtime tables.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important weaknesses in v1's empirical support and reproducibility. Appendix G supplies controlled evidence for the central control-variate mechanism and practical design choices, while the toy experiment directly tests distribution fitting. Appendices E–F make the implementation substantially more reproducible, and the bounded-action formulation explicitly preserves the intended target density. Headline optimality claims are also better qualified. Switching confidence intervals to seed ranges changes the uncertainty information available, but the validation and procedural clarity provide a substantial net improvement.
